https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/26/buda.text: Menü Kereső Pikó András szerint belátható időn belül javulhat Budapest közbiztonsága Belföld Mizsur András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „A kormány elfogadta a kerületi polgármesterek kezdeményezéseit, így belátható időn belül javulhat Budapest közbiztonsága” – írja Facebook-oldalán Pikó András józsefvárosi polgármester. Pósfai Gábor belügyminiszter 5 javaslat elfogadásáról számolt be a belső kerületek vezetőinek: 19 állandó és 90 visszatérő fővárosi helyszínen koncentrált lesz rendőri jelenlét. A kerületek azt kérik, hogy szeptemberi 15-ig jelöljék ki ezeket a helyszíneket. A kormány napirendre vette a Budapest-pótlék bevezetését a rendvédelmi dolgozók számára. Támogatják, hogy az önkormányzatok kapjanak valódi hatósági jogköröket a dohányboltok működésének szabályozására, az erről szóló kormányelőterjesztés előkészítése már zajlik. Az önkormányzatok olyan hatósági jogköröket szeretnének, amik lehetővé teszik a dohányboltok éjszakai nyitvatartásának a korlátozását, súlyos jogsértések esetén működésük felfüggesztését. Támogatják az objektív felelősség kiterjesztését a térfigyelő kamerával dokumentálható közlekedési jogsértésekre. A kerületek kérése, hogy a bírságokból származó bevétel az érintett önkormányzatokhoz kerüljön, mivel az önkormányzati rendészek végzik az intézkedéseket. Felülvizsgálják az éjjeli menedékhelyek működési rendjére vonatkozó javaslatot. Pikó szerint ezeken felül a Belügyminisztérium továbbá javaslatot fog tenni a Fővárosi Önkormányzati Rendészeti Igazgatóság (FÖRI) és a kerületi önkormányzati közterület-felügyeletek és rendészetek hatásköreinek kiterjesztésére is. „Üdvözöljük, hogy az új kormány elődjétől eltérően meghallja az önkormányzatok javaslatait és nyitott az együttműködésre a közös problémáink megoldása érdekében. […] Az elmúlt 16 év bűnös mulasztásainak következményeit nem lehet egyik napról a másikra kezelni, de biztosak vagyunk abban, hogy a kormány és az önkormányzatok együttműködésével lépésről lépésre hatékonyan javíthatjuk a közbiztonsági helyzetet is” – írta posztjában, amit Ferencváros, Terézváros, Erzsébetváros és a XIII. kerület polgármestere is aláírt. A budapesti belső kerületek vezetői nyár közepén kezdtek el arról kommunikálni, hogy érezhetően romlott a közbiztonság a fővárosban : agresszív szerhasználókra, kukákat felborogató palackgyűjtögetőkre, közterületeken letáborozó embercsapatokra panaszkodtak. Szerintük az vezetett ide, hogy a Fidesz kormányzása alatt leépült a pszichiátriai és addiktológiai ellátás, meggyengült a szociális intézményrendszer, a rendőrség pedig súlyos létszámhiánnyal küzd. A helyzet súlyossága miatt közös levélben fordultak a kormányhoz a kerületi polgármesterek. Erre reagálva a kormány 30 napos fokozott rendőri ellenőrzést rendelt el július közepén. Pósfai Gábor arról is beszélt, hogy életpályamodellel, a bérek rendezésével és visszaszereléssel oldanák meg az országos rendőrhiányt. A Budapesti Rendőr-főkapitányság és a Belügyminisztérium szerint Magyarországon kilencezer rendőr hiányzik, ebből több mint kétezer Budapestről. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Opposition leader Angus Taylor says a Coalition government would repeal several climate and renewable energy policies. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP View image in fullscreen Opposition leader Angus Taylor says a Coalition government would repeal several climate and renewable energy policies. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australian politics Angus Taylor pledges to repeal swathe of climate policies, saying ‘Australia has done its bit’ Several measures were previously introduced or supported by Coalition, prompting claim Liberals and Nationals would ‘let climate change rip’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales and Petra Stock Wed 23 Sep 2026 02.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 03.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Angus Taylor has vowed to repeal a raft of emissions reduction and renewable energy policies, including several measures supported by or introduced under past Coalition governments, within a month of being elected prime minister, prompting accusations he would “let climate change rip”. On Wednesday, Taylor’s energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, announced a new bill would be introduced to parliament within 30 days after a Coalition win at the next federal election to ensure affordable, reliable and secure energy to Australians. The bill, which contains a package of eight previously announced opposition policies, would remove safeguard mechanism and nuclear prohibitions, both introduced by previous Coalition governments. It would also: Scrap vehicle emissions standards . Remove the legislated net zero by 2050 target. Revoke four of six offshore wind energy zones due for completion by the late 2030s: the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury regions. Introduce a renewable energy code of conduct for developers. Require energy funding provided to states and territories prioritises energy affordability and reliability. Change the Australian Energy Regulator’s main focus to affordability and reliability. “Australia has done its bit,” Taylor said at a press conference when asked why it wanted to reverse laws driving down emissions. “What we will continue to see is technologies emerging with lower emissions that Australians want to choose. That is fine, and that is great.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Speaking at an energy forum on Wednesday, Tehan said the geopolitical changes in recent years, including the ongoing conflict over the strait of Hormuz, gave the Coalition the social licence to split energy from climate policy. “I think the Australian people, and you can feel it in the mood of the nation at the moment, want us to be much more sovereign, capable, be able to stand on our own two feet, and make sure that we can deal with the world with a strong economy,” he said. Tehan said the Coalition would “handle emissions reduction separately” with a policy released later this year. The energy minister, Chris Bowen , said the plan would take a “chainsaw to the economy and household budgets” and “make Australia poorer, weaker and less secure from global shocks”. “They want to take choice away from Australians – remove your ability to take control of your energy bills with a cheaper home battery, and pick a cheaper to run car,” he said. Bowen said the Coalition’s plan to “stop renewables and household batteries” and extend the life of existing coal power stations would mean households would be “left to pick up the bill of global shocks”. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, described it as a “One Nation policy with a Liberal Party sticker on it”. “Dan Tehan’s latest brain fade would put a wrecking ball through the economy,” he said. “This is a plan for a smaller economy, lower wages, poorer workers and fewer jobs.” The energy policy reversal was similarly criticised by Kooyong MP, Monique Ryan, and acting Greens leader, Mehreen Faruqi, for taking the country backwards. “The Coalition’s plan is dumb, dangerous, and desperate climate denial which would make energy more expensive and unreliable,” Dr Ryan said. Faruqi also took aim at Labor after its resources minister, Madeleine King, marked the opening of the Beetaloo basin with smiles. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Australians deserve a safe climate future, but we won’t see that while the Labor government is capitulating to fossil fuels and the Coalition’s energy policy is written to prop up corporate profits,” she said. 3:01 What is an El Niño and how could it cause the hottest year on record? – video Environment groups have condemned the Coalition’s announcement, with the Australian Conservation Foundation’s head of political advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, saying Australians deserved better. “You can’t be anti-renewables and pro-energy reliability, because renewables with storage is the most reliable and affordable form of energy, while nuclear is the most expensive and would need to be publicly funded,” McFadzean said. “To commit to slow the renewables transition is a breathtaking act of economic self-harm that would increase climate pollution and abandon jobs and investment in the future low carbon economy.” The chief executive of the Climate Council, Amanda McKenzie, described the energy announcement as “pure ideology” underpinned by years of climate denial. “The Coalition’s plan is to let climate change rip. It’s deadly negligence that would leave Australians facing more fires, floods and heatwaves,” she said. “The Coalition wants to force Australians back into the most polluting cars in the world and increase our dependence on foreign oil.” Farmers for Climate Action, a group representing more than 8,000 farmers across Australia, said they were “extremely disappointed”. Harden sheep and crop farmer and FCA spokesperson Peter Holding, said giving up on pollution reduction was crazy. “We are extremely disappointed in the Coalition today. You can’t say you’re looking after farmers while you axe pollution reduction policies, when we know more pollution means more fires and droughts, more climate change, and higher insurance costs,” he said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Ulrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party. Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/AP View image in fullscreen Ulrich Siegmund, right, congratulates Tobias Rausch on becoming president of the federal state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday. Both represent Germany’s far-right AfD party. Photograph: Jan Woitas/Pool DPA/AP Germany State parliament elects Germany’s first far-right speaker since second world war Tobias Rausch secures role of president in Saxony-Anhalt after AfD’s election breakthrough Europe live – latest updates Kate Connolly in Berlin Tue 6 Oct 2026 11.38 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 11.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Alternative für Deutschland has become Germany’s first far-right party to secure the position of speaker of a regional parliament since the second world war. Tobias Rausch, a former estate agent, was elected in the first round of voting on Tuesday in Saxony-Anhalt. He won 48 out of the 82 votes cast. Later in the day, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, part of the AfD’s more extreme wing, was elected as Rausch’s deputy. The AfD, which is classed as “rightwing extremist” by the eastern state’s intelligence agency, won nearly 44% of votes in elections last month , dealing a hammer blow to Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and his centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU). Rausch’s election to the role of president of the parliament – and its speaker – took place at the inaugural gathering of members in the state capital, Magdeburg. Twenty-nine voted against Rausch and five abstained. View image in fullscreen Protesters console each other outside the state parliament in Magdeburg after the election of Tobias Rausch as speaker on Tuesday. Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty Images The AfD parliamentary group holds 39 seats, narrowly short of an absolute majority. Five politicians from the BSW, a small leftwing party that echoes the AfD’s stances on Russia and immigration, had already said they would vote for Rausch. Tuesday’s result means that four other MPs voted for the 35-year-old in the secret ballot. The willingness of politicians to break the “firewall” – a moral agreement among other parties to shun the AfD – gives the party a chance of being able to form a government in the state – a feat it had looked unlikely to pull off. This would be even more of a historical watershed in postwar Germany. The BSW’s support for Rausch came after the party’s founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, declared it was time to do away with “firewall idiocy”. The party’s deputy leader, Christian Leye, said the “firewall is not working” and the votes of nearly 44% of electors could not be ignored. “We need an intelligent way of dealing with the AfD and that means dealing with the content of their programme instead of a firewall,” Leye told German media. View image in fullscreen Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in the state parliament after being elected deputy speaker on Tuesday. He is being lined up as Saxony-Anhalt’s culture and science minister. Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/Reuters It was not immediately clear who was behind Tillschneider’s election because the BSW had said it would refuse to vote for him. He received 44 votes. As the architect of the AfD’s “radical” manifesto, he is lined up to become culture and science minister in the state. He has referred to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as “a real man with a sound set of values” and accused immigrants of “streaming in here in masses … wanting to squander our money”. Tillschneider is a scholar of Islamic studies who has described Islam as a “fungus” growing on the “German oak”. His family emigrated from Romania to Germany in the 1980s. In his acceptance speech, Rausch promised to represent all voices and “take different opinions seriously and to try to take decisions in a transparent way”. He was applauded by his own parliamentary group and the ranks of the BSW. The other MPs did not respond. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Demonstrators read the German constitution during a protest outside Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament on Tuesday. Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty Images Rausch was one of the key figures in a nepotism scandal over AfD MPs employing family members in parliament. He denied claims that several of his siblings and a brother-in-law were working in the state parliament but confirmed he was employing several players from the football club where he is a member. He is a close ally and confidant of Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate, who is positioning himself to take over as leader of Saxony-Anhalt. He has yet to say which parties or politicians have agreed to cooperate with the AfD, only that “negotiations are going well”. The AfD claims to be courting members of the CDU to break the firewall, a claim CDU leaders deny. The BSW says it will support an AfD-led parliament only if a nonpartisan figure is appointed to lead it, a position the AfD rejects. Siegmund has until December to form a government. Opposition MPs raised alarm over the breaching of the firewall. “Whoever has invested a representative of extremist and anti-constitutional party with this office will bear responsibility for the consequences,” said Green MP Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, to loud applause. The result of the Saxony-Anhalt poll, along with two other regional elections in September, has piled huge pressure on Merz, who pledged on taking office in 2025 that he would halve the AfD’s support by boosting the economy and reducing immigration. Instead, the CDU’s support has more or less halved and that of the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls. Before the vote, Eva von Angern of the leftwing Die Linke party and the longest-serving member of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament, drew parallels between Rausch’s election to the post of speaker, and Hermann Göring’s use of that role in the Reichstag in the 1930s to facilitate Adolf Hitler’s rise to power. She claimed that the negative consequences of the AfD’s win in the state were already being felt in lower tourist numbers and teachers withdrawing job applications. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Erin Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson and the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, after a deadly mushroom-laced lunch at her home in rural Australia. Photograph: James Ross/AP View image in fullscreen Erin Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment for the murders of Don and Gail Patterson and Heather Wilkinson and the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, after a deadly mushroom-laced lunch at her home in rural Australia. Photograph: James Ross/AP Erin Patterson mushroom trial Erin Patterson to die in prison after losing bid to overturn mushroom murder convictions Victorian court of appeal rules Patterson should be jailed for life with no parole over deadly beef wellington lunch that killed three people Erin Patterson mushroom murders appeal – live updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Nino Bucci Justice and courts reporter Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.48 EDT First published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Erin Patterson has lost her bid to overturn her convictions and been resentenced to life behind bars with no chance of release, as Victoria’s highest court handed down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case . The court of appeal ruled on the two appeals on Friday, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August. Erin Patterson appeal live updates: Victorian woman loses bid to overturn triple-murder convictions over deadly mushroom-laced meal Read more Patterson, 52, did not attend the 15-minute court hearing in person, and showed no emotion on the video feed as McLeish outlined why her appeal had failed, and how the director of public prosecutions had succeeded in seeking a longer sentence. Patterson was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch. She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital. 1:21 Erin Patterson appeal: judges reject mushroom murderer's bid to overturn sentencing - video McLeish said the court had granted leave to appeal on the first two grounds of Patterson’s appeal, but dismissed the appeal, and dismissed the five other grounds raised by her lawyers. He said the court granted the DPP appeal against the sentence, however, as it was clear the original sentence did not properly reflect the seriousness of her offending. McLeish said Patterson sustained an intent to murder all four people for three weeks, from the time they were invited to the lunch, during the meal, and during the “protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted”. A visual guide to people involved in the story The offending was “carefully planned and deliberate”, he said, and involved an “elaborate series of deceptions” including claims that she had cancer, denying she had foraged mushrooms, and lying about the source of the mushrooms. “This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest possible terms,” McLeish said. When the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, and walked off-screen. In the courtroom, family members hugged and were emotional, and detectives involved in the case looked elated. Nobody commented outside court. Patterson now must apply to the high court for leave to appeal, should she wish to continue fighting her conviction or new sentence. She is one of only a handful of Victorian offenders sentenced to life without parole, and one of the only women in Australian history to be given the sentence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion In August, the court heard Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars. Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Richard Edney, for Patterson, had said the failure to properly separate the jury during their deliberations was a fundamental irregularity that had denied her a fair trial. “What we say has occurred here in the applicant’s trial was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure of a process,” Edney told the court in August. They also argued that the trial judge, Christopher Beale, erred in ruling that photos and videos related to mushrooms and found on an SD card in Patterson’s home was inadmissible, as it tended to support her evidence that she foraged for mushrooms. 1:24 Erin Patterson: Australia’s mushroom murderer sentenced to life in prison – video During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the DPP, said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient. When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court: “It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that. “But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.” Explore more on these topics Erin Patterson mushroom trial Victoria news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Erin Patterson to learn fate in appeal against mushroom murders convictions Erin Patterson cites ‘unfair and oppressive’ questioning and jury ‘irregularity’ in mushroom murder appeal Erin Patterson appeals guilty verdicts over deadly mushroom lunch that killed three Erin Patterson mushroom murders inspire new book by Helen Garner Erin Patterson: prosecutors to appeal ‘manifestly inadequate’ sentence for triple murderer Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://slguardian.org/nato-says-it-outm.text: Nato General Alexus Grynkewich: “To deter, we must show we are ready to act at any time.” Nato’s senior military commanders say the alliance possesses overwhelming conventional military superiority over Russia and is developing detailed plans to defeat any attack on its territory, as Russian sabotage, drone incursions and other hostile activities intensify concerns about European security. In an interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel, published in issue 43/2026, US General Alexus Grynkewich, Nato’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, and General Carsten Breuer, Germany’s chief of defence, described preparations for a potential conflict, including a three-stage strategy to repel attacks, weaken enemy forces and destroy the systems sustaining an offensive. Both commanders argued that maintaining credible deterrence, modernising armed forces and preserving transatlantic unity were essential to preventing a wider war. “Our military capabilities, which we would deploy in a major conflict, far exceed Moscow’s by a wide margin,” Grynkewich said, describing Nato’s conventional advantage in a war involving the full alliance. He cited the alliance’s F-35 fighter aircraft and its larger numbers of modern destroyers and submarines as capabilities Russia could not match. Grynkewich, 55, commands Nato’s allied forces in Europe and all US forces stationed on the continent. He spoke to Der Spiegel at the alliance’s operational headquarters in Mons, Belgium, alongside Breuer, 61, who is due to become chairman of Nato’s influential Military Committee in the summer of 2027. The interview came amid reports of Russian drones entering Nato airspace, aggressive manoeuvres by the Russian navy and an alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport. Breuer said Germany had quickly attributed the suspected attack on the airport to Russia and received support from Nato allies within hours. He described the response as evidence of the alliance’s strength and cohesion. Grynkewich said the suspected operation itself represented a crossing of a boundary. Had it succeeded, several fully fuelled Antonov aircraft could have exploded, potentially causing deaths. He argued that governments should pay greater attention to the risks Russia was prepared to take to inflict damage, rather than focusing exclusively on the risks associated with their own responses. Both generals rejected suggestions that the possibility of conflict should deter continued support for Ukraine. Grynkewich said Russian President Vladimir Putin wanted European and American populations to fear that assisting Kyiv could lead to war with Russia. Breuer added that Moscow was also attempting to drive a wedge between European Nato members and the United States, warning that alliance unity must be preserved. They also differed in emphasis over terminology used to describe Russian activities. Grynkewich said he preferred precise operational terms such as sabotage, arson and terrorist attacks to the broader description of hybrid warfare. Breuer said the term “shadow war”, recently used by Martin Jäger, president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, helped convey the seriousness of developments and avoid language that minimised their significance. Grynkewich maintained that Russia was unlikely to launch a large-scale conventional attack against Europe because Nato’s deterrent capabilities made direct confrontation unattractive. Breuer said the threat nevertheless depended on three factors: Moscow’s willingness to use military force, its growing military capabilities and an opportunity created by weakness among its opponents. Nato, he argued, must ensure that Russia perceived no such weakness. The alliance’s response includes a strategy Grynkewich called its “theory of victory”, organised around three stages: “to block, to blunt and to break”. Nato forces would first block incursions into allied territory using land forces, aircraft and naval assets. If attacks continued, they would weaken the opposing forces through artillery and air strikes against their first and second lines. A third stage would target command posts, supply routes, defence industries and the wider system supporting the attack. “We will immediately and decisively repel and destroy an attack,” Grynkewich said. He described the strategy as a framework for ensuring that member states understood their responsibilities and could respond without delay. Breuer said it would guide Germany’s forces, including its 45th Brigade stationed in Lithuania, while retaining the flexibility needed to adapt to changing battlefield conditions. The Suwalki Corridor, which connects the Baltic states with the rest of Nato territory, remains a central consideration in eastern-flank planning. Breuer compared its strategic importance with the Fulda Gap, a potential invasion route from the former Soviet Union during the Cold War. Grynkewich said Nato’s exercises were intended to demonstrate readiness rather than signal aggression, adding that the alliance monitored Russian activities without overreacting. Drone warfare presents another urgent challenge. Grynkewich said Nato needed large quantities of inexpensive one-way attack drones, cheaper cruise missiles and stronger defences against unmanned aircraft. Lessons from the war in Ukraine and the conflict with Iran had exposed shortcomings in drone interception, he said, but Nato had developed plans for integrated sensor and interception systems. The alliance is working closely with Ukraine, whose battlefield experience has informed military procurement and industrial cooperation. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius signed an agreement on joint combat-drone production with his Ukrainian counterpart in April. Grynkewich cited Merops drones, developed in Ukraine and now being integrated into US forces, as an example of the cooperation. Breuer said Nato procurement was also becoming faster. Systems classified as medium-range loitering ammunition could reach troops within nine or ten months, compared with the years such processes would normally take. Grynkewich said the alliance was studying Ukraine’s system for transmitting soldiers’ operational feedback directly to industry. Concerns persist among Baltic states about whether the alliance would respond decisively to Russian aggression, particularly under US President Donald Trump. Grynkewich pointed to the Nato summit’s closing declaration in Ankara, saying every member had reaffirmed its commitment to collective defence. Recalling Trump’s description of the summit atmosphere as “full of love”, he said the president’s words reflected the collective determination he had witnessed among the allies.
